Binary search. A fundamental computer science algorithm for finding a target value within a sorted list or array by repeatedly dividing the search space in half. With a time complexity of O of log n, binary search exemplifies the power of divide-and-conquer. By eliminating half the remaining candidates with each comparison, it achieves exponential speedup over naive linear search, especially on large datasets. Binary search works only on sorted data. At each step, it compares the target to the middle element and discards either the upper or lower half of the remaining search space, rapidly converging on the target or confirming its absence. The algorithm's time complexity is O of log n, meaning searching a million-element array requires at most approximately twenty comparisons. This logarithmic scaling makes it vastly faster than linear search, which is O of n and requires up to a million comparisons. Binary search is a canonical example of divide-and-conquer. The problem is recursively split into smaller subproblems—the left or right half—each solved in the same way, demonstrating how strategic problem decomposition yields exponential efficiency gains. The algorithm requires that the underlying data structure, usually an array or list, supports random access, or O of one lookup by index. Linked lists are unsuitable for binary search because accessing the middle element requires O of n traversal. Binary search trees, or BSTs, generalize binary search into a data structure where every node's left subtree contains smaller values and the right subtree contains larger values, enabling efficient search, insertion, and deletion in O of log n average case time. Variants exist for partially sorted data, finding boundaries such as the smallest element greater than or equal to a target, and approximate searching. Lower-bound and upper-bound functions in programming libraries implement these variants. Binary search is ubiquitous in practice. Database indexing uses binary search to quickly locate records. Version control systems use it to find the commit that introduced a bug, a process known as git bisect. Hardware design leverages logarithmic search efficiency in various contexts. Binary search is a canonical computer science algorithm and exemplifies the divide-and-conquer algorithmic strategy. Its time complexity, O of log n, characterizes it precisely and is analyzed using Big O notation, the mathematical framework for analyzing algorithm efficiency. The algorithm requires sorted input, which sorting algorithms provide. The logarithm function characterizes its time complexity mathematically. Arrays and binary search trees are the data structures enabling binary search. The algorithm is often implemented recursively, dividing the problem recursively in each step.
